hooks.text: A single blinking star once destroyed the entire known universe.
The universe grew a billion times larger because of one photograph.
In 1920, the entire universe was just one single galaxy.

title: The Star That Destroyed the Universe
description: In 1923, a single pulsing star in Andromeda proved that our galaxy was just a tiny part of a much larger cosmos.

beats.text: A single blinking star once destroyed the entire known universe.
beats.visual: Wide-field photograph of the Andromeda Galaxy, M31

beats.text: In 1920, astronomer Harlow Shapley argued the Milky Way was the only galaxy in existence.
beats.visual: Portrait photograph of astronomer Harlow Shapley, circa 1920

beats.text: Heber Curtis countered that fuzzy spiral clouds were actually distant, independent island universes.
beats.visual: Portrait photograph of astronomer Heber Curtis, circa 1920

beats.text: In October 1923, Edwin Hubble used the 100-inch Hooker Telescope to photograph the Andromeda Nebula.
beats.visual: The 100-inch Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson Observatory

beats.text: He spotted a changing star, V1, that proved Andromeda was roughly one million light-years away.
beats.visual: Edwin Hubble's 1923 photographic plate of Andromeda showing the star V1

beats.text: That distance was far outside the Milky Way, instantly making the cosmos billions of times larger.
beats.visual: Artist's conception of the Milky Way galaxy from a distance

beats.text: Shapley read Hubble's letter and told a colleague, "Here is the letter that destroyed my universe."

card.big: Here is the letter that destroyed my universe.

beats.text: Everything we knew about our home changed because a single blinking star once destroyed the entire known universe.
beats.visual: Telescopic view of the Andromeda Galaxy

better_than_last: Applied a strong contradiction hook and a precise scale ladder structure to improve 10% retention and average view duration.
